title: Evening with family
hook: kirtan, a sakhi, a talk at home
tomorrow: what does a bedtime prayer have to do with a wedding?

segments.voice: Yesterday, evening Rehras: the morning's question comes back at dusk. The day put down, at that door. After that, the house.
screen: `THE DAY PUT DOWN.` → `AFTER THAT, THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Dishes done, phones mostly face down, kirtan playing low from a speaker in the corner. In some Sikh homes this is when a story gets told. Tonight's: Guru Nanak stays with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter, and turns down a feast from Malik Bhago, a rich official. Called to explain, the Guru takes Lalo's plain bread in one hand and Bhago's rich food in the other, and squeezes. From Lalo's bread, milk. From Bhago's, blood. The kids go quiet. Then the smallest one asks: did that really happen?
screen: `DISHES DONE, KIRTAN ON.` → `LALO'S BREAD, BHAGO'S FEAST.` → `DID THAT REALLY HAPPEN?`

segments.voice: Sikh families answer that question in more than one way. One view: tell it as it's told. The sakhis are how Guru Nanak has been handed down at kitchen tables, generation to generation, and a child who hears the milk and the blood remembers forever where honest bread comes from. A story doesn't have to be cross-examined to do its work, and the elders who told it meant it. Another view: tell the lesson, and mark the source. Some Sikh teachers point out that the janamsakhis were written down after the Guru's time, by different hands, and aren't Gurbani. So they tell the miracle as a picture of honest earning against wealth squeezed out of others, and point to what the Granth itself says. And the Granth does name him. On ang 722, Guru Nanak addresses a hymn to Lalo by name. In paraphrase: as the Lord's word comes to me, so I speak it, Lalo. The friendship is in the Guru's own words. The milk and blood are in the sakhi. Either way, look at what fills the room: music, a story, a question, and the talk that follows. That's an evening with family.
screen: `DID IT REALLY HAPPEN?` · `ONE VIEW: TELL IT AS IT'S TOLD.` · `ANOTHER: TELL THE LESSON.` · `ANG 722: THE GURU NAMES LALO.` · then, large: `HOME FILLS UP.`

segments.voice: Pick one story worth telling at home: a sakhi, or one from your own family. Say its first two lines out loud now, the way you'd start it at the table. Then let the sit hold the rest of it.
Evening with family. Kirtan, a sakhi and a talk at home, when the day is over.
Your line: home fills up. Music, a story, a question at the table. Sleep well, when it comes.

howItsDone: In Sikh homes evenings may include kirtan, recorded or sung, the telling of sakhis from the Gurus' lives, and talk about Gurbani; families differ on how they tell the miracle stories of the janamsakhis to children.

fork.setup: your cousin wants to tell her kids the Lalo story with the miracle, just as Bebe told it. you'd rather tell the lesson. before you argue, what's her best case?
options: the sakhis are how the Guru was handed down; a child keeps the milk and blood for life.
the milk and the blood are written in the Granth, so the scene can't be questioned.
kids can't follow a lesson at all, so only the magic part will stick in their heads.
fork.reveal: that's the strongest version of the first view. the second view has its case too: the janamsakhis aren't Gurbani, and the Granth names Lalo on ang 722.
